input.question: How is lead parts per million tested in soil?
input.ground_truth: There are several analytical tools one can use to determine the concentration of trace metals including [Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS)](_URL_3_) [Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (AES)](_URL_1_) [Mass Spectrometry](_URL_2_) It is commonplace for all of these methods to build 'calibration curves' using the [standard addition method](_URL_0_), or by some other methods.

Question: How is lead parts per million tested in soil?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the soil is like a big chocolate cake. Now, we want to know if there are tiny, tiny pieces of lead (like the metal, not the pencil kind) mixed in the cake.

To check this, scientists take a little bit of the soil (like taking a small bite of cake). They put it in a special science kitchen (called a lab). There, they use magic tools (machines) that can count how many tiny pieces of lead are hiding in that little bite.

They count how many lead pieces are in one million tiny pieces of the soil. That’s what “parts per million” means. If there are too many lead pieces, it’s not safe to play in that soil. If there are only a few, it might be okay.

So, they test the soil to see if there’s too much lead hiding in it, just like checking if there’s too much salt in your cake!
